title: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
titleZh: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
author: speckx
relevanceReason: 命中 5 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC.

The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions. The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.

comments.author: Silfen
comments.textRawHtml:
Reading this thread makes me realize that seemingly no one has heard the basic, mundane case for why Nvidia would want to do so much "circular financing" as a matter of totally normal business strategy. This may not be the whole story, but it's worth understanding.

Because of bottlenecks in the supply chain, Nvidia knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory. They could raise prices quite a bit more, but then their only customers would be hyperscalers (building competing chips) and possibly OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia is willing to forgo present day profits for the strategic value of keeping its customer base diverse and promoting the network effects of e.g. CUDA. Instead of quoting a lower price per GPU to neoclouds and startups, they finance purchases of chips, but the two are roughly equivalent (financing means Nvidia takes on more risk, but has more upside and locks in future demand). It is in their commercial interest to have many competing buyers of their chips.

Obviously this creates fun mechanisms for fraud and wacky accounting (and I'm agnostic as to whether that's happening here), but it's worth knowing about the boring/obvious story before donning your tinfoil hat.

children.author: pvab3
children.textRawHtml:
>In Berlin during a conference, Huang, accompanied by his top sales executives, broadcast a new message to a half-dozen CEOs of companies that are major buyers of Nvidia chips who were seated around a circular table. He opened with a story that sounded like a fable, according to people who attended. Huang had once found a soup vendor in Japan, he said, with a long line of customers. He joined the line, and after a long wait, enjoyed one of the best bowls of soup he’d ever had. When he asked for another serving, the soup-seller told him no—he had too many customers waiting and not enough soup for all of them.

“He’s a better businessperson than all of you,” Huang told the cloud computing CEOs. The soup-man doesn’t sell out all his inventory to one or two customers, but instead keeps prices high and his customer base diverse, the CEO said.

“You are not establishing the value of my products,” he said.

children.author: keeda
children.textRawHtml:
Hehehe my pet theory is that Jensen was using exactly the opposite strategy to secure that “avalanche of chips and wafers” from TSMC: Nvidia’s monopoly cash flows give it the volume and money to secure its massive supply-chain advantage by buying priority amongst TSMC’s customers.

That is, Jensen is going to the TSMC soup seller and saying “I’ll buy 80% of all your soup for twice the price because people are willing to pay 10x that with my ramen noodles in it.” And TSMC being the real bottleneck in this industry, knows there’s really nowhere else for its other customers to go. It of course, wants to keep all customers happy… but some will get much more soup than others.

This is probably a huge factor in keeping their advantage over their customers and competitors (but I repeat myself.) That is, TPUs and Trainium etc simply cannot acquire the necessary volume of chips at a competitive enough price-point to put a dent in Nvidia’s grip on the market. But the hyperscalers need all that compute NOW NOW NOW, so they have no choice but to turn around and begrudgingly pay Nvidia for that supply. Which puts more cash flow in Nvidia’s pocket, which buys them more soup, and on this loop continues.

children.author: lizknope
children.textRawHtml:
> Nvidia knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory.

The WSJ article is basically saying the opposite. The hyperscalers are making their own chips and they are buying less from Nvidia.

https://archive.is/20261113091227/https://www.wsj.com/tech/j...

This is my comment in another part of this thread

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50493251#50496483

> Then he went on to describe the situation the company was in. Major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia, making plans to use alternative chips and lessen their reliance on the firm. Even worse, Huang said, the vast supply of chip wafers and memory Nvidia had committed to buying were coming at him like an “avalanche.”

Jensen's son-in-law was making these vendor financed deals and Kress the CFO now interim CEO was against them.

Large customers like Nvidia and Apple want billions of chips. TSMC can't just ramp up and down instantly. It takes 3+ years and $30 billion to build a modern fab. So TSMC has contracts where you are commiting to buy the wafers for years in advance.

I've worked for multiple fabless chip companies that use TSMC to manufacture. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and the other big hyperscalers are making their own AI chips to move away from Nvidia. The startups like OpenAI are doing the same so the real demand for Nvidia chips is dropping. But Nvidia can't easily get out of the contracts with TSMC to manufacture and buy the chips. They would probably have multi billion penalties that would show up on their financial statements.

Some people think Nvidia is acting as a VC fund for AI startups but my view is that Jensen freaked out about the dropping demand for Nvidia chips. So he is funding these startups with circular finance deals to buy the Nvidia chips that he can't sell to the hyperscalers anymore.

children.author: retwakm4
children.textRawHtml:
The Hyperscalers are often working with a company like Broadcom (the elephant in the room on this topic) to design said chips. They don't usually have the amount of ASIC and Networking and Optics hardware expertise in house that would be required. See, for instance, Google's TPUs. Broadcom's hardware people are world class and some of the best paid in the business. It's the most elite hardware company in a lot of ways in terms of total comp for top engineers.

Google hires some hardware people to come up with general requirements for specialized stuff like ASICs, then sends those requirements to Broadcom to do the hard parts and negotiates big multi-billion dollar contracts with them. OpenAI did the same and contracted Broadcom after liking what they saw with the TPUs. There are several other Broadcom customers that I'm probably not at liberty to disclose.

But no, as far as GPU replacements are concerned, the Hyperscalers generally are not experienced enough in the specific types of hardware required to do this by themselves. It's very specialized and boutique high price work and more difficult than say, designing an ARM chip (something a company like Amazon or Google could probably handle in house).

In general though, yes, I agree. Hyperscalers are trying to reduce dependence on NVIDIA. Many are quite far along in their ASIC projects (Google especially, they are on their 8th generation TPU! Way past just being a small scale experiment by now.) and have large volumes of them running in place of NVIDIA chips and much more efficiently already.

Broadcom is fabless, and uses TSMC for these sorts of chips. They are mostly a boutique design "mercenary" firm for exactly this sort of specialized hardware for Hyperscaler customers and other clients that run significant amounts of infrastructure in house (so, think JP Morgan for instance). That's the core of their business, along with increasingly Infrastructure Software in the form of virtualization and mainframes and private and hybrid cloud (so some natural sales overlap there, just generally, "big companies that need specialized big data center hardware and software").
